headline: You build backend systems through small, reviewable steps, with tests, explicit trade-offs, and a rollback plan close at hand.

archetype.name: The Rollback Architect
archetype.description: You treat implementation as a sequence of decisions that should be explainable, testable, and reversible. Your prompts move from hypotheses and alternatives to tightly scoped changes, then to operational checks and durable documentation. Even a working solution still owes you evidence about concurrency, correctness, and production behavior.

dimensions.title: Small steps, explicit gates
dimensions.summary: You establish a plan or baseline before changing behavior, then advance through narrowly scoped steps. Tests and rollback checks are part of the work itself, especially around migrations, transactions, and refactoring.

evidence.quote: Good plan. Let's start with step 1 only: the database migration.
Before we refactor the invoice generator, write characterization tests that pin down the current behaviour.
Add a test that proves the webhook is not written when the transaction rolls back.

dimensions.title: Brief instructions, durable decisions
dimensions.summary: You give concise directions with clear boundaries and specific output formats. You also ask for decisions and procedures to become reusable artifacts, from ADRs to runbooks and issue templates.

evidence.quote: Write the migration and a rollback. Do not touch the handlers yet.
Document the decision in an ADR.
Turn the checklist into a GitHub issue template.

dimensions.title: Transactional backend focus
dimensions.summary: Your requests center on Go, PostgreSQL, and billing or ledger behavior. You engage directly with locking, database constraints, transaction isolation, and domain edge cases rather than leaving correctness implicit.

evidence.quote: Review this Go function for race conditions. Explain your reasoning step by step.
Use a deferred constraint trigger. Write the SQL and property-based tests with rapid.
Run through the edge cases again: leap years, currency rounding, negative line items.

dimensions.title: Production behavior matters
dimensions.summary: You repeatedly focus on safe operations: rollout verification, delivery guarantees, observability, and rollback. Performance claims also need something measurable, such as metrics or benchmarks.

evidence.quote: The runbook should include a verification step after each stage and a rollback section.
Add a section about exactly-once vs at-least-once delivery and how consumers should deduplicate.
Let's keep the mutex. Add a benchmark so we can compare later.

dimensions.title: Understand before choosing
dimensions.summary: You use the assistant to investigate mechanisms and compare alternatives before committing to changes. Your learning questions are concrete: why a concurrent test flakes, how isolation levels differ, or what a synchronization choice costs.

evidence.quote: The test for concurrent requests is flaky. Can you explain why before changing anything?
What are the trade-offs between using a mutex here and a channel?
Explain how this behaves under READ COMMITTED versus SERIALIZABLE.

traits.name: Deliberate scope control
traits.description: You keep changes small and make their boundaries explicit, giving yourself clear opportunities to inspect each step.

evidence.quote: Good plan. Let's start with step 1 only: the database migration.
Now break the rollout into PR-sized steps.
Now refactor in small commits, one concern per commit, and tell me the commit messages first.

traits.name: Correctness needs proof
traits.description: You ask tests to establish behavior and failure guarantees, including the awkward cases around transactions and existing code.

evidence.quote: Keep it under 80 lines and add tests first.
Add a test that proves the webhook is not written when the transaction rolls back.
Before we refactor the invoice generator, write characterization tests that pin down the current behaviour.

traits.name: Reasoning before repair
traits.description: You want a causal explanation or comparison before a fix earns your approval. The assistant serves as an investigation partner as well as an implementer.

evidence.quote: The test for concurrent requests is flaky. Can you explain why before changing anything?
We need to rotate the database credentials without downtime. Propose two approaches and compare them.
Help me form hypotheses before we look at code.

traits.name: Operational follow-through
traits.description: You carry work beyond implementation into verification, alerting, and recovery. Production readiness needs concrete checks.

evidence.quote: The runbook should include a verification step after each stage and a rollback section.
Write the migration with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and a check that it is valid afterwards.
Add alerting thresholds and explain how you chose them.

traits.name: Decisions deserve a paper trail
traits.description: You turn technical reasoning into structured documents that other people can review and reuse.

evidence.quote: Go with the dual-credential approach. Write a runbook in docs/runbooks/rotate-db-creds.md.
Document the decision in an ADR.
Write a design doc for moving webhooks to an outbox pattern. Sections: context, goals, non-goals, design, alternatives, rollout.

funFacts: Your 36 prompts span 11 sessions: compact conversations with plenty of follow-through.
Your median prompt length is 85 characters. Scope control applies to sentences, too.
Your busiest hours are tied: 09:00 and 10:00 each contain 13 prompts in Europe/Berlin time.
Your project tally is 29 prompts for billing-service and 7 for ledger.
